title: Prop
description: What a thing standing in the district looks like. A prop is a sim entity that is neither a body nor a carried item -- a container, a bed, a campfire, the well -- and this is the entry that says how it draws, per CLAUDE.md's 'how a thing looks is content, not code'. Nothing in sim/ reads this file: the sim knows a `searchable`/`bed`/`campfire`/`water_source` component and nothing about pictures, and presentation/appearance.gd's PROP_KINDS is the one table mapping a component (and the one boolean that changes its look -- searched, lit) onto an id here. NOTE: the content validator is shallow -- top-level types and unexpected top-level keys only -- and does not recurse into `appearance`; check_appearance.gd is the gate that checks the block's inner shape, and check_topdown.gd is the one that proves the draw loop reads it.

id.description: Stable namespaced id, always prop.<thing>, with a state suffix where one boolean changes the look (prop.container.searched, prop.campfire.lit). Two ids rather than one entry with two tints, because a state that draws differently is a different picture and this keeps the resolver a lookup rather than a branch.

name.description: Human-readable name. Not shown to the player -- SimContainers.hud_clause and needs.hud_clause own the prose; this is for whoever is reading the content.

appearance.description: Same block as a zombie's or a survivor's, plus the two keys a prop needs because it draws as a footprint on the ground rather than as a pawn. A prop with a `sprite` draws the art and ignores `shape` and `size`. The `anyOf` is the whole rule: `tint` was flatly required here until props had art, because a prop with neither would be an invisible thing standing in the world -- but a prop that declares a tint *and* a sprite has that tint multiplied over every pixel of the art (appearance.gd's `modulate_for`), so demanding one of art would have stained all of it. Required-unless-sprite is the shape that keeps the original guarantee -- every prop draws as something -- without forcing the stain. NOTE that neither validator enforces this: the Godot one is shallow and never recurses into `appearance`, and the frozen TypeScript oracle loads schemas only for its own six content types, of which `prop` is not one. check_appearance.gd's prop lane is the enforcement, in both directions.

sprite.description: Registry key for assets/sprites/<key>.png, 64x64 centre-anchored. Every shipped prop declares one; the shapes below remain the supported floor for a prop authored without art, not a stopgap.

tint.description: The colour the shape draws in, and the modulate on a sprite if one is declared -- which is why a prop with art declares no tint: it would multiply the art. Required unless `sprite` is (see the anyOf above): a prop with neither would be an invisible thing standing in the world, which is the defect this content type exists to end.

shape.description: Which of the renderer's ground-footprint primitives draws this prop when it has no art: box (a bevelled square -- a crate, a cupboard), slab (a long rectangle with a pale band at the head -- a bed), disc (a filled circle with a darker core -- a fire pit), ring (an annulus -- a well). Geometry, not identity: the vocabulary is presentation's and check_topdown.gd asserts main.gd actually draws every name in it.

size.description: Footprint as a fraction of a tile, longest side. Defaults to Appearance.PROP_SIZE when absent. _draw_prop reads it only on the procedural path -- art is blitted at one tile -- but it is not decoration once a prop has art: check_appearance.gd measures the sprite's opaque bounding box against size x 64, so this number is what the picture was authored to and a bed drawn the size of a crate fails the build.
